title: Pretesting Enhances Learning in the Classroom https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1174/217119711794394635
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 21, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises Soderstrom and Bjork's classroom study on pretesting, giving students short, low-stakes multiple-choice tests before a lecture covers the material. In an undergraduate research methods course, pretested topics showed significantly better final exam performance than non-pretested control topics, and the benefit even extended to related-but-not-pretested material. Barton draws out the two proposed mechanisms: pretesting appears to sharpen attentional processing when the material is later covered in class, and it seems to prompt more self-regulated study outside class among students unsure of their pretest performance. He notes that feedback wasn't given immediately after the pretest, since correct answers were embedded in the following lecture instead, suggesting immediate feedback isn't a necessary ingredient for the effect, while flagging that classroom research is inherently less controlled than the lab studies pretesting is usually built on.
points: Short, low-stakes multiple-choice pretests before a lecture significantly improved final exam scores — both for pretested topics and for related material that wasn't directly pretested.
Immediate feedback after the pretest doesn't appear necessary; students in the study only learned the correct answers when the lecture covered them later.
Pretesting seems to work through two mechanisms — sharper attention during the subsequent lecture, and more self-directed study outside class among students unsure of their answers.
Teachers can build their own pretests or ask students to self-generate pretest questions, even though most students report never having tried the technique before.
quotes: The results of the study found that pretesting significantly improved student learning, both for the material tested and for related material that was not pretested.
The authors suggest that the primary mechanism responsible for the pretesting effect is enhanced attentional processing during class and enhanced self-regulated study outside of class.
Providing immediate feedback after pretests may not be necessary for achieving learning benefits.
Teachers can implement short, low-stakes pretests before lectures to enhance student learning.
Teachers should encourage self-testing and pretesting as study strategies for their students.
Thus, not only was final exam performance better for information that had been previously pretested, but this benefit also extended to information that was related to such material.
